questions.q: In the opening example, why did adding "opay" to the Provider union not produce a compile error in feeKobo?
questions.explain: A default that returns a real value answers silently for kinds it has never heard of. Either end with an exhaustive check (provider satisfies never) or put the behaviour in an object that must implement every method.
options: Because unions are not checked inside switch statements
Because the default branch handles every value not listed, including new ones, so the function still returns a number for all inputs
Because feeKobo returns number, which includes 0
Because "opay" was added after the function was compiled

questions.q: What is the main purpose of encapsulation?
questions.explain: An invariant, such as "the balance is never negative" or "balance equals the ledger", can only be guaranteed if nothing outside the object can change the state around the methods that enforce it.
options: To hide code from other developers
To make objects faster
To make the object's own methods the only way to change its state, so they can keep its invariants true
To make every property readonly

questions.q: A getter returns the object's internal array typed as readonly LedgerEntry[]. What can still go wrong?
questions.explain: The type stops typed callers, but the value is the object's own array. Return a copy, or a frozen copy, so the object stays the only owner of its state.
options: Nothing; readonly arrays cannot be changed
Untyped code or a cast can still push into the real internal array, because readonly only exists in the compiler
The array is copied on every access, which is slow
TypeScript refuses to compile a getter that returns a private field

questions.q: Which kind of private field is also enforced at runtime?
questions.explain: private is a compile-time check that is erased. # fields are a JavaScript feature: code outside the class cannot read them at all, even with a cast.
options: TypeScript's private balanceKobo
JavaScript's #balanceKobo
Both
Neither; privacy is always compile-time only

questions.q: The checkout needs payment providers. Whose view should the PaymentProvider interface be written from?
questions.explain: An interface written for the caller stays stable when providers change, and every provider can implement it honestly. An interface copied from one SDK forces every other provider to pretend to be that one.
options: The most popular provider's SDK, copied as closely as possible
The checkout's: only the operations and data the checkout needs, in its own terms
The database's, so it can be stored directly
Every provider's, with a method for each feature any of them has

questions.q: Bank transfers cannot be refunded automatically. What is the best way to model refunds?
questions.explain: Small interfaces that each mean something (interface segregation) keep implementers honest. Callers that need refunds ask for PaymentProvider & Refunds or check with canRefund, and the compiler stops code that assumes every provider can refund.
options: Put refund in PaymentProvider and throw "not supported" in the bank-transfer provider
Put refund in PaymentProvider and return undefined for bank transfers
Put refund in its own Refunds interface, implemented only by providers that can refund, and check the capability with a type guard
Remove refunds from the system

questions.q: An object literal { name, charge, feeKobo } with the right types is assigned to a PaymentProvider variable. Does it need implements or a class?
questions.explain: Structural typing: anything with the right members is a PaymentProvider. implements adds no code; it moves the check to where the class is declared.
options: Yes, only classes can implement interfaces
No; TypeScript checks interfaces by shape, and implements only asks for that check on a class declaration
Yes, it must be created with Object.create
No, but it must be cast with as PaymentProvider

questions.q: class Money { readonly #checked = true; constructor(readonly kobo: number) {} }. Why does payout({ kobo: 0.5 }) fail when payout expects a Money?
questions.explain: Private members make a class behave nominally. That guarantees every Money went through the constructor, where it can be validated. The compiler knows nothing about the value 0.5.
options: Because 0.5 is not an integer
Because a class with a private member is only compatible with its own instances; an object literal cannot supply #checked
Because interfaces cannot have readonly properties
Because payout is not generic

questions.q: A base class implements feeKobo using this.percent() and this.capKobo(), which subclasses supply. What is this pattern called?
questions.explain: The base class fixes the algorithm (percentage with a cap) and subclasses fill in the steps. It is the most defensible use of inheritance, and still couples every subclass to the base class's algorithm.
options: Decorator
Template method
Adapter
Composition root

questions.q: What does the override keyword add?
questions.explain: Without it, a renamed parent method turns the child's method into an unrelated new method that nobody calls. override is erased from the output; it only adds the check.
options: It calls the parent method automatically
A compile-time check that the parent really has that member, so renaming or removing it in the parent makes every override an error
It makes the method final
It changes the method's runtime behaviour

questions.q: What does noImplicitOverride in tsconfig.json enforce?
questions.explain: It makes every override visible in the code, so readers know a method replaces inherited behaviour, and a rename in the parent is always caught.
options: That subclasses cannot override anything
That a method replacing a parent's method must be marked override
That abstract methods need a body
That every class has a parent

questions.q: SavingsWallet extends Wallet overrides withdraw to throw for amounts over ₦50,000. It compiles. What principle does it break?
questions.explain: The override's types match, so the compiler is satisfied. The behaviour does not: a subclass must accept at least what the parent accepts and keep its guarantees. Only tests, such as contract tests, can check that.
options: Encapsulation
Interface segregation
Liskov substitution: code written for any Wallet breaks when given this subclass, because it added a precondition Wallet never had
Dependency inversion

questions.q: Which is a sound way to support withdrawal limits?
questions.explain: If callers must respect a limit, the abstraction must tell them about it. Otherwise the subclass is not really a Wallet and should not claim to be one.
options: Keep SavingsWallet extends Wallet and document the limit
Make the limit part of the abstraction (for example a maxWithdrawalKobo every wallet has, which callers respect), or stop making savings wallets substitutable for wallets
Catch every RangeError in callers
Mark withdraw as override

questions.q: What makes await provider.charge(amount, email) polymorphic?
questions.explain: Polymorphism means one piece of code works with many kinds of object. With interfaces it needs no inheritance: Paystack's class and the bank-transfer object literal both work.
options: The await
The same call works for any object that implements PaymentProvider, and each object decides what charging means
The method name is the same in every class because of inheritance
TypeScript generates one version of the call per provider

questions.q: withRetry(channel) returns a new NotificationChannel that calls channel.send up to N times. Why is this better than a RetryingSmsChannel extends SmsChannel class?
questions.explain: Wrapping objects that share an interface (the decorator pattern) combines freely: withFallback(withRetry(sms, 2), email). With inheritance, SmsWithRetry, EmailWithRetry, SmsWithRetryAndFallback… multiply.
options: Because classes cannot retry
Because the wrapper works for any channel and combines with other wrappers, instead of needing a subclass for every combination of channel and behaviour
Because functions are faster than classes
Because inheritance cannot call parent methods

questions.q: In dependency inversion, which module owns the PaymentProvider interface?
questions.explain: The abstraction belongs to the code with the business rules. Adapters import it and implement it, so imports point toward the checkout, and a change in a provider's API only changes its adapter.
options: The Paystack adapter
The checkout, the high-level code that uses it
A separate package from each provider
Whichever module was written first

questions.q: Which file should import the concrete PaystackAdapter class?
questions.explain: If only one place knows concrete classes, swapping a provider or using a fake in tests changes only that place. A DI container automates this wiring; it does not change the direction of the imports.
options: Every file that charges a payment
The checkout service
Only the composition root (for example main.ts), which creates the concrete objects and passes them in
The interfaces file
No file; it should be loaded dynamically

questions.q: A class implements PaymentProvider and its charge method returns { reference, status: "success" } without a return type annotation. Why does it fail the implements check?
questions.explain: implements checks the finished class; it does not guide inference inside it. Annotate the method's return type (Promise<ChargeResult>) so the literal is checked against the union.
options: Because async methods cannot implement interfaces
Because implements does not contextually type the class's methods, so "success" widens to string, which is not a valid status
Because object literals are not allowed in classes
Because reference is missing

questions.q: The payment succeeds, then sending the SMS receipt fails. What should the checkout do?
questions.explain: The money has moved; that fact must not be lost or undone because a secondary step failed. Retrying the whole payment could charge the customer twice.
options: Throw, so the caller retries the whole payment
Refund the payment
Record the successful payment and report the notification failure separately, for example notified: false
Ignore the failure silently

questions.q: What is a contract test?
questions.explain: The compiler checks that implementations have the right types; a contract test checks they keep the interface's promises (fees never negative, references never empty). It is the Liskov principle turned into a test.
options: A test that checks a legal agreement
One set of behavioural checks written against an interface and run against every implementation, including fakes
A type test with Expect<Equal<…>>
A test that only runs in production

questions.q: Which change is cheaper in the functional design (a discriminated union plus functions) than in the object-oriented one?
questions.explain: A new operation is one new function with one switch. In the class design, every class must gain the method. For a new kind, it is the other way round. That trade-off is the expression problem.
options: Adding a new payment provider
Adding a new operation, such as refundWindowDays(provider)
Letting a plugin add its own provider
Keeping a stateful connection per provider

questions.q: Other teams must be able to add notification channels without editing your module. Which design fits?
questions.explain: An interface is an open set: anyone can implement it without touching your code. A union is a closed set that only its owner can extend.
options: A discriminated union of channel kinds with a switch in send
A NotificationChannel interface that their objects implement
An enum of channel names
A class hierarchy they must extend

questions.q: Which part of a shop is usually the better fit for plain data and functions?
questions.explain: Closed sets of data that travel across boundaries serialize cleanly and grow by operations: a union with functions fits. Stateful adapters to the outside world fit objects behind interfaces.
options: A database connection pool
A payment provider adapter with API keys and retries
Promotion rules that are stored in the database, sent through APIs, and gain new reports more often than new kinds
A WebSocket connection to a courier

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1.5% of 2,000,000 is 30,000, plus 10,000 gives 40,000, under the 200,000 cap. OPay falls into default and silently gets a zero fee, which the compiler never questioned.
options: paystack:40000 flutterwave:28000 opay:0
paystack:40000 flutterwave:28000 opay:undefined
paystack:30000 flutterwave:28000 opay:0
paystack:40000 flutterwave:28000

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The getter returned the real internal array, so the cast let outside code add an item that was never paid for. The # fields were never touched; the invariant broke anyway.
options: TypeError: Cannot add property 1, object is not extensible

questions.q: Now the getter returns Object.freeze([...this.#items]). What does this print?
questions.explain: Pushing into a frozen array throws a TypeError in strict mode, and the internal array was never exposed anyway. Each access creates a new copy, so two reads are different arrays.
options:
true
1 false

true
1 true
2 false

false
1 false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: TypeScript's private is erased, so pin is an ordinary property that serializes, a real leak. The # field is truly private and is not serialized at all. Methods never are. Objects need explicit conversion at boundaries.
options: {"owner":"Ada","pin":"1234"} [ 'owner', 'pin' ]
{"owner":"Ada"} [ 'owner' ]
{"owner":"Ada","balanceKobo":500000} [ 'owner', 'balanceKobo' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: emptyInto is correct for a Wallet, and the subclass compiles, but it adds a rule the parent never had. The same call now fails for one kind of wallet: a Liskov substitution violation that no type error reports.
options: moved 8000000 | RangeError: limit is ₦50,000
moved 8000000 | moved 8000000
moved 8000000 | RangeError: insufficient funds
RangeError: limit is ₦50,000 | RangeError: limit is ₦50,000

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a retry, the first failure goes straight to the fallback; the next message succeeds on SMS. With withRetry(sms, 2), the second attempt succeeds, so the fallback is never used. The order of wrapping decides the behaviour.
options:
email:A sms:B
sms:C

sms:A sms:B
sms:C

email:A email:B
email:C

email:A sms:B
email:C

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1.5% of 20,000,000 is 300,000, capped at 200,000 for Paystack. 1.4% is 280,000, capped at Flutterwave's own 250,000. The base class calls the subclass's capKobo, which is what makes the template method work.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The guard checks the capability at runtime, and in the true branch the compiler knows refund exists. A provider without the capability gets a normal business answer instead of a crash.
options:
paystack REF-9-R
bank-transfer manual refund needed

paystack manual refund needed
bank-transfer manual refund needed

paystack REF-9-R
bank-transfer REF-9-R
TypeError: provider.refund is not a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both fit the interface by shape, so both work in the same array and the same loop. instanceof checks the runtime prototype chain, which only the class instance has. Interfaces do not exist at runtime at all, so you cannot use instanceof PaymentProvider.
options: paystack=15000,bank-transfer=5000 [ true, false ]
paystack=15000,bank-transfer=5000 [ true, true ]
paystack=15000 [ true ]
paystack=15000,bank-transfer=5000 [ false, false ]

questions.q: Finish withdraw so the wallet's balance can never go negative: throw new RangeError("insufficient funds") when the amount is larger than the balance, and new RangeError("amount must be positive") when it is not a positive number. The program should print the three lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: The checks run before the state changes, so a failed withdrawal leaves the wallet untouched. A negative withdrawal would otherwise increase the balance. !(amountKobo > 0) also rejects NaN.
questions.expected:
ok, balance 300000
RangeError: insufficient funds
RangeError: amount must be positive

questions.q: Finish the decorator withRetry(channel, attempts): it returns a Channel whose send calls channel.send up to attempts times and rethrows the last error. The program should print sent: order shipped after 3 tries.
questions.explain: The decorator returns a new object with the same interface that holds the original. It works for any Channel, and can itself be wrapped by other decorators.

questions.q: Finish the type guard canRefund and refundOrManual: providers with a refund method refund automatically, others return "manual refund needed for REF". The program should print PSK_1-R manual refund needed for TRF_9.
questions.explain: Refunding is a capability, checked at runtime and narrowed at compile time. After the early return, provider is PaymentProvider & Refunds, so provider.refund is typed.
questions.expected: PSK_1-R manual refund needed for TRF_9

questions.q: Add a class Opay to the template method below: 1.25% fee, capped at 150,000 kobo. Use override for the cap. The program should print 12500 150000.
questions.explain: The subclass supplies the two steps and inherits the algorithm. override makes the compiler confirm that capKobo really exists in the parent.

questions.q: Finish providerContract(provider): for each amount in [100, 250_000, 50_000_000], report a failure when the fee is not a non-negative whole number, or when it is at least the amount. Return the failure messages. The program should print paystack OK and bank-transfer fee for 100 is 5000.
questions.explain: The same behavioural checks run against every implementation of the interface. The compiler already guaranteed feeKobo exists and returns a number; the contract checks that the number makes sense.
questions.expected:
paystack OK
bank-transfer fee for 100 is 5000

questions.q: Objects lose their private state in JSON. Finish toData() (returns plain data) and the static fromData(data) (validates and rebuilds a wallet, throwing new RangeError("invalid balance") for a negative or non-integer balance). The program should print the expected lines.
questions.explain: Converting at the edges keeps objects for behaviour and plain data for travel. fromData is the only way back in, so it validates, exactly like a constructor guards an invariant.
